question: A 28-year-old patient presents with progressive skin changes as shown in the clinical images below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

clinicalImages.caption: Bilateral hand and foot involvement
clinicalImages.description: Well-demarcated patches of depigmentation affecting hands and feet

explanation.A: CORRECT - Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition causing loss of melanocytes and consequent depigmentation. Key features visible in the images include: well-demarcated patches of complete depigmentation, symmetrical distribution affecting face, hands and feet (common sites), and the characteristic perioral involvement. The bilateral pattern and typical locations strongly support this diagnosis.
explanation.B: INCORRECT - Pityriasis versicolor typically presents with scaly, hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches that are not completely depigmented. It's caused by Malassezia fungus and commonly affects the trunk, not the typical vitiligo distribution shown.
explanation.C: INCORRECT - Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation usually follows inflammatory skin conditions and tends to be irregular in shape and distribution. The symmetrical, well-demarcated pattern shown in the images is not typical of post-inflammatory changes.
explanation.D: INCORRECT - Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis presents as small, punctate white spots, typically on sun-exposed areas of elderly patients. The large, confluent patches shown in the images are not characteristic of this condition.
explanation.E: INCORRECT - Chemical leukoderma results from contact with depigmenting chemicals and typically shows an asymmetrical pattern related to the site of chemical exposure. The symmetrical bilateral pattern shown is not consistent with chemical-induced depigmentation.

mnemonic: VITILIGO features: Visible depigmentation, Immune-mediated, Typical locations (face/hands/feet), Increasing with stress/trauma, Loss of melanocytes, Inherited predisposition, Gradual progression, Outline well-demarcated

question: A 25-year-old patient presents with hair loss as shown in the clinical images. What is the most likely diagnosis?

clinicalImages.caption: Scalp involvement - circular patch
clinicalImages.description: Well-demarcated circular area of complete hair loss with smooth scalp

clinicalImages.caption: Exclamation mark hairs at edge
clinicalImages.description: Characteristic short, broken hairs at the periphery of the patch

clinicalImages.caption: More extensive involvement
clinicalImages.description: Multiple confluent patches of hair loss

explanation.A: CORRECT - Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition causing well-demarcated patches of complete hair loss. Key diagnostic features visible include: perfectly round or oval patches of complete hair loss, smooth scalp surface without scaling or inflammation, characteristic 'exclamation mark' hairs at the periphery (short, broken hairs), and the typical presentation in a young adult.
explanation.B: INCORRECT - Androgenetic alopecia shows a gradual, progressive pattern of hair thinning, typically with frontal hairline recession and crown thinning in men, or diffuse thinning in women. It doesn't present as discrete circular patches.
explanation.C: INCORRECT - Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) typically shows irregular patches with hairs of varying lengths due to repeated pulling. The perfectly round, smooth patches shown are not consistent with trichotillomania.
explanation.D: INCORRECT - Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) usually presents with scaling, inflammation, and broken hair shafts. The smooth, non-inflamed scalp surface shown in the images makes fungal infection unlikely.
explanation.E: INCORRECT - Telogen effluvium causes diffuse hair thinning across the entire scalp following a triggering event. It doesn't present as localized circular patches of complete hair loss.

mnemonic: ALOPECIA features: Autoimmune etiology, Loss in circular patches, Occurring at any age, Patches well-demarcated, Exclamation mark hairs, Complete hair loss, Inflammation absent, Affects 1% population
